documents.abstract: Instruction-guided 3D editing is essential for interactive content creation, yet it faces a significant bottleneck: the severe scarcity of high-quality paired training data. Existing approaches attempt to bypass this by either relying on slow test-time optimization or training on pseudo-pairs constructed via complex pipelines, which often introduce structural drift and geometric artifacts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that learns feed-forward 3D editing without paired 3D supervision via Generative Prior Distillation. Instead of relying on ground-truth 3D pairs, our core idea is to distill visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from powerful foundation models directly into a 3D editing model. Specifically, through a differentiable rendering pipeline, we supervise the 3D representation using two complementary signals: a 2D visual prior from an image editing model at the main editing view, and a semantic prior from a Vision-Language Model at novel views to ensure strict instruction following and source identity preservation. Crucially, to address the geometric collapse and multi-view inconsistencies inherent in 2D projection supervision, we introduce a 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization. Acting as a geometric prior, this term operates in the 3D latent space, constraining the edited output to remain within the manifold of realistic 3D assets defined by a pretrained image to 3D teacher model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior instruction fidelity and cross-view consistency, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Our project is available at: https://github.com/thiamine128/PriorEdit3D.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: The advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) transformed technology’s role in the education sector by introducing highly adaptive, interactive tools. Standard implementations are often inadequately designed to effectively aid students. In some cases, these systems hinder genuine learning by inducing cognitive offloading, offering immediate solutions that bypass the cognitive processes necessary for deep conceptual understanding. This concern highlights the need for pedagogically grounded systems that foster genuine understanding and skills development. To address this gap, this paper presents an experimental implementation evaluating the feasibility of embedding formal educational frameworks directly into AI system architecture. We introduce Learning Companion, a prototype engineered to mitigate passive cognitive offloading by translating educational theory into programmatic workflows. Rather than replacing educators or automating learning, the Learning Companion is designed to strengthen meaningful learning interactions by positioning AI as a collaborative partner that supports learner agency through guided dialogue and adaptive instructional scaffolding. Aimed at enhancing critical reasoning and academic writing, the system operationalises Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) through algorithmic Socratic questioning to provide structured instructional scaffolding. This human-centred approach demonstrates how AI can complement teaching and foster deeper learner engagement while preserving meaningful connections between students, educators, and intelligent learning technologies.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence can produce convincing misleading text and synthetic media, raising questions about how people assess and respond to online information. This study examines self-reported awareness of possible legal consequences and three distinct responses to potentially false content: considering harm before forwarding, reporting deceptive material and correcting or removing content later found false. It analyses 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records from a Bangladesh sample comprising law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents. Because the questionnaire does not measure the frequency of exposure to AI misinformation or observed social media activity, the study assesses stated awareness and self-reported practices rather than exposure or actual conduct. Items are analysed separately using descriptive distributions, paired comparisons and exploratory Spearman correlations with Holm adjustment. Legal-consequence awareness was endorsed by 244 respondents (63.4%); consideration of harm by 269 (69.9%); reporting by 268 (69.6%); and correction or removal by 259 (67.3%). Awareness and reporting showed a small positive rank correlation (ρ = .138), whereas the relationships with harm consideration and correction were uncertain after adjustment for three tests. Differences between correlation coefficients require direct comparison; statistical significance in one association alone does not demonstrate a difference across practices. The findings do not show that legal awareness causes responsible behaviour. The article integrates information credibility, media literacy and the theory of planned behaviour as perspectives for a future study with measured exposure, validated items and observed verification tasks.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Objective: to study national and international approaches to regulating the operation of autonomous vehicles in order to determine the appropriate legal form of international unification and systematization of legislation in the field of autonomous transport. Methods: the methodological basis of the work was formed by a doctrinallegal approach combined with general scientific methods of cognition, including analysis and synthesis, induction and deduction, systemicstructural and formal-legal approaches. The main special method was comparative-legal one. It allowed classifying the national regulatory models of individual jurisdictions and comparing modern international legal acts developed by relevant international organizations in relation to various types of autonomous transport. Results: the study identified and characterized four regulatory approaches of states to the legalization of autonomous vehicles: the adoption of policies and strategic documents, the adaptation of current transport legislation, the introduction of experimental legal regimes, and the adoption of special laws on autonomous vehicles. It was proved that overcoming the fragmentation of legal regulation, strengthening public trust in artificial intelligence technologies and coordinating the interests of the state, business and consumers is difficult to achieve through the mechanical incorporation of disparate acts, and this requires codification. It was shown that a single codified act based on sectoral principles can ensure internal consistency of norms, unity of terminology and consolidation of the rights, duties and guarantees of subjects at the stages of design, certification, implementation and commercial operation of autonomous systems. This conclusion is confirmed by an analysis of the initiatives of the World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations of the UN Economic Commission for Europe and the International Maritime Organization. Scientific novelty: a theoretical-legal concept of systematization and codification of legislation on autonomous vehicles was developed. The concept integrates the principles of public law – transparency, accountability and protection of public interests – into the mechanism of legal regulation of intelligent transport systems. A three-level system of balancing public, private and interstate interests is substantiated. The study proposes object areas and structural parameters of a unified code covering issues of legal liability, security certification and data management. Practical significance: the formulated conclusions and proposals can serve as a methodological basis for overcoming regulatory gaps and eliminating collisions that can stifle technological innovation or pose threats to road and maritime safety. The results can be used by national legislators and international regulators in designing codified acts that provide legal certainty for manufacturers and operators of autonomous vehicles while maintaining state supervision and protecting citizens’ rights.

Objective: to study current technological and legal concepts in order to determine the legal nature of content moderation in social networks, choose appropriate means of its regulatory regulation, and establish the boundaries of government interference in the activities of digital platforms. Methods: the methodological basis of the work was a set of general scientific methods of cognition (analysis, synthesis, induction and deduction) in combination with special legal methods, including formallegal and comparative-legal. The use of the comparative-legal method made it possible to compare the regulatory models of Russia, China, the European Union, and the United States. The interdisciplinary approach allowed evaluating algorithmic filtering and commercial moderation from the standpoint of public-law and civilistic doctrines. Results: it is proved that moderation of user content is an element of corporate governance of a social network and an integral part of its business model. It was established that, in legal terms, this activity is implemented in three aspects: as a public-law instrument for suppressing the dissemination of illegal content in the interests of state and public safety; as a constitutional-legal guarantee of freedom of speech and fundamental rights of citizens; as a private-law mechanism for protecting the property and personal non-property rights of users and online communities. It is proved that, under hybrid information filtering with artificial intelligence algorithms, the legitimacy of platform control is achieved by a combination of legislative regulation, corporate selfregulation and, user self-censorship. Scientific novelty: the study formulates the concept of balancing the publiclaw goals of suppressing illegal information and protecting the private interests of digital content creators while limiting the discretionary powers of platform owners. The applicability of a private-law approach to content moderation relations is substantiated, including when transferring the functions of checking and blocking materials to external contractors on outsourcing terms, where a third party is actually given public-law powers without direct contractual relations with the user. The article substantiates considering artificial intelligence in the moderation circuit as an element of a sociotechnical system that affects public trust and reliability of the information environment. Practical significance: this is due to the presence of gaps in legislation regarding the regulation of platform moderation procedures, as well as the lack of regulatory certainty of the user’s right to receive an explanation of the reasons for restricting access to content and the right to challenge the decisions of algorithmic systems or moderators. The formulated conclusions can be used by the legislator and operators of digital platforms in improving the legal mechanisms of transparency, accountability and proportionality of content moderation in social networks.

Breast cancer (BC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, driven largely by tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and therapeutic resistance. Tissue biopsy, while the diagnostic gold standard, offers only a static snapshot of a constantly evolving disease, and repeated sampling is often impractical, particularly in metastatic settings. Liquid biopsy has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative capable of capturing this evolving biology in real time through circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), and extracellular vesicles (EVs). This review examines the biological features, analytical technologies, and clinical applications of these analytes in BC, with particular attention to two rapidly evolving areas. First, we discuss how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being applied to multi-analyte liquid biopsy data, from methylation- and fragmentomics-based classifiers for early detection to models integrating ctDNA and CTC information for resistance profiling and treatment-response prediction, while critically examining current limits in clinical validation and interpretability. Second, we address the role of serial ctDNA monitoring in the neoadjuvant setting, where it can refine risk stratification beyond pathologic complete response and identify candidates for early therapeutic escalation, reflected in intervention trials now testing this approach prospectively. We also cover established roles of these analytes in treatment monitoring, minimal residual disease (MRD) detection, resistance tracking, and metastatic disease management, alongside persistent barriers to routine adoption, including limited early-stage ctDNA shedding, clonal hematopoiesis, and inconsistent analytical standardization. As these technologies mature, liquid biopsy is poised to move from a prognostic tool toward one that guides personalized treatment in BC. Not applicable. This article is a narrative review. Liquid biopsy enables longitudinal profiling of breast cancer biology. ctDNA, CTCs, and EVs provide complementary biological information. ctDNA detection can precede breast cancer relapse by approximately 10–12 months. PADA-1 showed improved PFS with plasma-guided ESR1-directed switching. Multi-analyte approaches may improve prediction beyond single biomarkers.

Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
An LLM-automated workflow built on uncertainty-guided cascade Gaussian process regression screens 4900 TMX 4 @G structures. DFT confirms six stable single-atom HER catalysts with η HER < 0.15 V.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased questions about whether a final code artefact alone can constitute sufficient evidence of student learning in programming education. This poster presents a practice-based evaluation of a redesigned second-year programming unit that incorporated multiple forms of evidence of learning. The assessment design is informed by authentic assessment (Boud & Molloy, 2013), feedback for learning (Carless & Boud, 2018) and self-explanation theory (Chi et al., 1989). It responded to current calls for assessment reform in the age of AI by shifting attention from the final artefact to the processes through which students design, explain, test and improve code (Lodge et al., 2023). Across three progressively sequenced assessments, students produced working Python programs, submitted WakaTime development records, recorded video explanations of design decisions, declared and justified GenAI use where permitted, and revisited prior code to improve exception handling and pytest testing. GenAI was allowed under accountable-use conditions, during which students were required to identify GenAI-assisted code, ensure that their submissions used concepts taught in the unit, and demonstrate that they understood and could explain the code they submitted. Assessment 1 established foundational object-oriented programming practices. Assessment 2 asked students to build a weather-data bot using CSV data, web scraping, datetime, logging, collections and pandas analysis. Assessment 3 required students to return to their Assessment 2 codebase and use feedback from Assessment 2 to strengthen its robustness through built-in exceptions, custom exceptions and tests. The design operationalised process-oriented assessment at task level. Code provided product evidence; WakaTime provided process evidence; video explanation provided conceptual evidence; and feedback with staged task design supported iterative development. Together, these tasks created an evidentiary architecture that made programming processes, conceptual reasoning and judgement more visible than final code alone. The evaluation drew on 68 anonymous unit feedback responses. Open-ended feedback was examined using thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017). Three student-perception themes were emergent. First, authentic tasks positioned programming as professional practice: students valued project-based tasks such as CSV analysis, web scraping and data-processing bots because they resembled meaningful programming work. Second, explanation and process evidence made computational thinking visible: students described shifts from writing code to thinking in terms of modularity, validation, debugging and engineering practice. Third, feedback supported iterative improvement and confidence: students reported that feedback helped them identify errors, revise code and progress more independently. The poster argues that process-oriented programming assessment should not rely only on restricting AI use. Instead, assessment can require multiple forms of evidence to validate student learning (Dawson et al., 2024) such as working code, development traces, self-explanatory video, feedback uptake, accountable AI-use declarations and testing artefacts. Video explanation is especially important because it prompts students to justify programing structures, methods, strategies and data-analysis approaches (Lai & Niblock, 2024). The study is limited by its reliance on one unit, one teaching period and self-reported student feedback. Further analysis of WakaTime data, video explanations, code revisions and pytest artefacts will examine how process evidence relates to conceptual understanding, reasoning and feedback uptake.

Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts memos, summarises meetings, translates messages, analyses employee sentiment and answers customers, placing it at the centre of how managers communicate. This paper examines how these developments are reshaping management communication and what they demand of managers. Using a documented integrative review of 49 sources from management, organisational communication and human–computer interaction, it integrates media richness, sensemaking, sociotechnical systems and organisational trust theories into a multi-level account. A consolidated evidence table and a comparative analysis of seven AI applications show that AI improves the speed, clarity and reach of routine, informational communication, but that messages perceived as heavily AI-written lower judgements of the sender's sincerity, authenticity and trustworthiness, especially for relational and high-stakes messages, and that disclosure alone does not remove this penalty. The paper argues that AI changes the mechanics of management communication more readily than its meaning. It examines the Nigerian context in depth, including infrastructure, linguistic diversity, high power distance and the 2025 data protection directive, together with implementation barriers at technological, organisational, individual, cultural and regulatory levels. It then proposes the Human-Centred AI Communication (HCAIC) framework and positions it against existing frameworks. HCAIC comprises six practices (strategic intent, human oversight, authenticity and transparency, ethical data governance, capability building and employee participation), which act through perceived authenticity, message accuracy and psychological safety to produce trust, clarity and employee voice. Key concepts are operationalised and seven propositions are offered for empirical testing. The paper concludes that the defining managerial competence of the AI era is not generating messages, but making messages mean something to people.

Background: Increasing volumes of heterogeneous digital-health intelligence challenge conventional horizon-scanning methods and their ability to examine how technologies, clinical priorities and innovation pathways evolve over time. This study developed an agentic AI-assisted methodology for longitudinal digital-health horizon scanning. Methods: We analysed 123 NHS horizon scans conducted in 2015 and annually from 2019 to 2026, comprising 4,039 company-year profiles. Horizon-scan records were integrated with policy, clinical, funding and media evidence. Entity harmonisation, transformer-based semantic representations, TF-IDF analysis, machine learning and semantic clustering were used to characterise thematic evolution and estimate next-year corpus reappearance and future documented maturity. Performance was evaluated using nested company-grouped and rolling-origin validation, and candidate themes were contextualised through human-reviewed multi-agent synthesis. Results: The corpus shifted from enterprise, workforce and operational technologies towards condition-specific clinical applications, including oncology, women’s health, cardiovascular care, cognitive assessment, neurodevelopmental conditions and imaging artificial intelligence. Under nested company-grouped validation, XGBoost estimated next-year corpus reappearance with an F1 score of 0.67, ROC-AUC of 0.89 and average precision of 0.72. Extra Trees estimated future documented maturity with R2=0.40and RMSE =0.96, compared with R2=0.27and RMSE =1.05for direct carry-forward. Chronological performance was more variable across annual cohorts. Conclusions: The framework provides a structured and traceable approach for transforming historical horizon scans into longitudinal thematic intelligence, company-level estimates and candidate areas for further investigation. It is intended to augment expert-led horizon scanning rather than replace clinical, regulatory, procurement or commissioning judgement.

documents.abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

Abstract Foundation models for partial differential equations adapt efficiently to new tasks, but their effect on the original pretraining distribution is rarely measured. We study this retention problem on Poseidon, a neural operator pretrained on periodicdomain compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes families. We adapt it to two regimes absent from pretraining, a compressible Kelvin–Helmholtz flow and wall-bounded flow past a circular cylinder. Fine-tuning adapts efficiently but degrades the pretraining families. LoRA still forgets substantially, and freezing the whole trunk reduces forgetting without preventing it. We show that low-weight replay and joint training resolve this trade-off, extending the model to the new regimes while keeping the pretraining families near their original accuracy. These results suggest that lightweight replay can extend a PDE foundation model while substantially preserving its existing capabilities.

The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.

As higher education continues to rapidly digitise with the rise of Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL), the challenge is not only technology implementation or access, but meaningful integration into student-facing learning, assessment, communication and support practices (Chung et al., 2026). Despite increasing investment in TEL, research and practice continues to focus on technology adoption, functionality and efficiency (Feng et al., 2025; Wu & Chen, 2025). Consequently, learning technologies, pedagogy and student services are often treated as separate domains rather than interconnected components of an educational ecosystem (Barrett & Harte, 2023; Børte & Lillejord, 2024). This creates a design problem where students experience fragmentation across systems, processes and support services, leading to disconnection between learning and assessment. Drawing on practice-based evidence and relevant literature, this poster argues that advancing TEL requires intentionally designing connection across the educational ecosystem. This poster employs a practice-based, reflective methodology informed by evidence gathered across two intersecting roles at a research-intensive metropolitan university in Australia. First, as an educational developer involved in learning design, digital assessment implementation, and academic capability development. Second, as a strategic student experience officer within a stakeholder relations team, focused on cross-functional collaboration, service design, stakeholder engagement, and student support. Insights were drawn from implementation observations on digital assessment initiatives, stakeholder interactions across faculties and central service divisions, service-design challenges and student support queries. Recent literature on digital transformation, TEL, student wellbeing, and connected learning ecosystems was used to sensitise and critically inform these reflections, providing a conceptual lens through which patterns and gaps could be identified. This contributed to the development of a conceptual framework that positions learning, support, and technology as interconnected components of a connected educational ecosystem. Insights from the roles highlighted recurring points of disconnection in student facing practices, including assessment processes, support pathways and learning design decisions. These issues emerged at the intersections between academic, professional and technological domains, and were often reinforced by siloed approaches to working. These practice-informed reflections suggest that the future of digital learning depends on the intentional design of connection across students, educators, professional staff, and institutional systems. When learning, assessment, and support are designed in isolation, misalignment and fragmentation can occur, with implications for student success, satisfaction, and motivation (Bull, 2025; Liang et al., 2024). The implications on TEL are to prioritise collaborative connections across student-facing practices. To address the disconnect gap, the poster proposes a “Connection by Design” framework, developed through an iterative process of reflective analysis, stakeholder consultation, and engagement with literature on TEL, student wellbeing, digital transformation and connected learning. Practice-based observations from digital assessment implementation, service design initiatives, stakeholder interactions, support queries, and communication challenges were compared against themes from relevant literature and refined through ongoing professional dialogue, peer feedback, and cross-functional collaboration. This process contributed to the identification of three interdependent dimensions of effective TEL design. The first is human connection, which focuses designing learning and assessment that promote clarity, belonging and productive cognitive engagement (Zhou & Ye, 2024). The second is collaborative connection, which highlights the importance of co-design between academics, education designers and technologists and professional staff. The third is systemic connection, which involves the alignment of digital platforms and services through integration, policy coherence and embedded support pathways. Together, these three dimensions provide a practical approach for diagnosing disconnection and informing more connected, collaborative and human-centred TEL design.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) influencers’ wider adoption makes addressing the risks of perceived information manipulation crucial. This study employs a mixed-methods approach to investigate the antecedents and consequences of perceived information manipulation by AI influencers. Drawing on Hunt-Vitell Theory and Goal-Framing Theory, a theoretical model is tested using survey data from 625 participants in Singapore. The results indicate that reasonable use, privacy protection, non-deception, personal development, and perceived enjoyment significantly reduce perceived information manipulation, while informed consent has a negative but non-significant effect. Perceived information manipulation negatively impacts both routine and infusion use. Thematic analysis of 15 follow-up semi-structured interviews generates meta-inferences that provide both confirmation and complementary insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying the quantitative results. Based on these findings, this study offers practical recommendations for AI influencer operators and policymakers to mitigate potential negative social impacts, enabling the ethical realization of AI influencers’ full potential.

The purpose of the present study was to understand how meaningful work and vocational calling may benefit employees’ work and well-being under circumstances of job stressors. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources framework, we tested a model linking stressor exposure to work and health outcomes through one’s experience of meaningful work, and dependent on one’s perception of work calling via a two time-point survey of 493 employees. Exposure to particular stressors and evaluated workplace and health-relevant outcomes were consistently linked, and further support was found for the role of calling in buffering the impact of certain stressors on outcomes through work meaning. This study contributes to the occupational health and career development literatures by expanding our understanding of detriments to job-related (i.e., job satisfaction and turnover intentions) and well-being-related (i.e., physical symptoms and burnout) criterion variables from workplace stressors. Implications for organizations and counselors, study limitations, and future directions are discussed.

Scene perception for situational awareness is crucial for autonomous agents like UGVs and UAVs that involves sensing from different 2D and 3D modalities to execute tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection. However, UGVs and UAVs face limitations in power and computation capacity. To address these challenges, we propose an offloading framework called MobHeteroCAS , designed to leverage nearby peer autonomous vehicles for computation. Our framework addresses key challenges in offloading DNN (Deep Neural Networks) tasks in a collaborative environment: (a) Optimally offloading data/features to leverage nearby devices’ computation capabilities; (b) Reducing offloaded data for efficient communication in low-bandwidth environments; (c) MobHeteroCAS determines the optimal ”split ratio” to determine how much data should be offloaded to each nearby device based on network parameters such as RSSI values, latency incurred due to network conditions, workload, memory constraints (CPU, GPU, RAM), and power limitations. The key contribution of MobHeteroCAS is determining the optimal split ratio in stationary and mobile environments. Apart from the devices consuming more power and memory when they are mobile, the latency increases when the distance between communicating devices increases. Thus, MobHeteroCAS estimate the latency to offload the computation when devices are on mobile before selecting the optimal split ratio. MobHeteroCAS is truly fault-tolerant, incorporating the identification of device (agent) failure and task redistribution when a device fails. We empirically demonstrate that offloading DNN features instead of raw images reduces overall system latency. Therefore, we offload feature representations of raw images for tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation. In our study, we utilize a testbed comprising three Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) and one Linux laptop, implementing a self-adaptive optimization framework capable of managing multiple heterogeneous tasks collaboratively across multiple nodes. Our evaluations, involving simultaneous execution of multiple DNN tasks like Image Classification and Semantic Segmentation, demonstrate that employing a split ratio of 30%-42%-28% (data distribution across auxiliary nodes) reduces offloading latency by approximately 72% (from 38 \(ms/data\) to 10.5 \(ms/data\) ) compared to compressed frames and reduces total operation time by approximately 99% (from 281.33 minutes to 169 seconds) compared to the baseline configuration (execution on the primary node) in stationary setting. The latency improves by 78-82%.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for generative recommendation, where recommended items are generated directly from users' interaction histories. To further improve recommendation quality, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to align these models with recommendation objectives. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar rewards to implicitly guide exploration. These rewards do not specify which aspects of a candidate conflict with the user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. To address this gap, we propose VerRec, a verbalized feedback-guided RL framework for generative recommendation. Specifically, a user simulator generates personalized verbalized feedback based on the user's historical preferences and the candidate item profile. The policy uses this feedback to produce refined recommendations. Original and refined candidates form an expanded group and are jointly optimized with group relative policy optimization. The user simulator is only required during training and is removed at inference time. Experiments on three Amazon review datasets with two generative recommendation backbones demonstrate that VerRec improves recommendation accuracy and ranking quality. Further analyses show that verbalized guidance encourages exploration of more diverse candidates and helps the policy discover more rewarding recommendations during training.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

documents.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

Accurate biomedical image classification under limited supervision remains challenging due to scarce annotations, subtle inter-class differences, and complex disease semantics. Pretrained vision-language models offer a promising foundation for alleviating data scarcity through knowledge transfer, yet effectively adapting them to low-resource biomedical tasks remains nontrivial. To this end, we propose Multi-View Synergistic Learning (MVSL), a unified framework that jointly considers three complementary perspectives: adaptation paradigms, representation granularity, and disease semantic relationships. Specifically, MVSL adopts tailored adaptation strategies for visual and textual encoders, accommodating their distinct representational characteristics while preserving pretrained knowledge. To capture both holistic image semantics and localized pathological evidence, we introduce multi-granularity contrastive learning that aligns global image representations and local visual features with disease-specific textual embeddings. Furthermore, we develop a Disease Semantic Graph (DSG) that leverages disease descriptions generated by large language models to model class-level semantic relationships and regularize adapted textual representations, thereby complementing discriminative learning and helping mitigate excessive specialization toward observed categories. Through the synergy of these complementary perspectives, MVSL enhances fine-grained discrimination while supporting semantic consistency and generalization to unseen categories. Extensive experiments on 11 public biomedical datasets spanning 9 imaging modalities and 10 anatomical regions demonstrate the effectiveness of MVSL in few-shot classification and base-to-novel generalization. The implementation and detailed experimental results are publicly available at https://github.com/luoxiaoliu/MVSL.

Background Dietary, behavioral, psychological, and engagement resources may jointly be associated with survival in later life. We examined the association between a multidimensional ageing reserve (MDAR) index and all-cause mortality among older Chinese adults. Methods The 2008–2009 baseline data from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS) were linked to subsequent mortality records. MDAR combined four equally weighted standardized domains: dietary diversity, lifestyle behavior, psychosocial wellbeing, and activity/social-cognitive engagement. Follow-up was censored at 10 years. Cox models compared MDAR quartiles and estimated a linear summary association per standard deviation (SD). Restricted cubic splines assessed non-linearity. Complete-case analyses were supplemented by multiple imputation, a 2-year landmark analysis, attained-age models, and weighted analyses. Results Among the 10,249 participants (mean age 85.2 years; 53.7% women), 6,569 deaths occurred over 51,534 person-years. Fully adjusted hazard ratios (HRs; 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) relative to the lowest quartile were 0.94 (0.88–1.01), 0.99 (0.92–1.06), and 0.85 (0.78–0.93) for quartiles 2, 3, and 4, respectively. The linear summary hazard ratio per SD was 0.93 (0.90–0.96). The spline indicated non-linearity ( p = 0.007), with a more pronounced inverse association at higher scores. Activity and social-cognitive engagement had the clearest association in mutually adjusted domain models (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.89–0.95). The pooled estimate after covariate multiple imputation was 0.93 (0.90–0.96); the 2-year landmark estimate was 0.95 (0.91–0.99). Conclusion Higher MDAR was associated with lower mortality, particularly at higher score levels. The association weakened after adjusting for health, function, and cognition. Selection, residual confounding, and overlap between the index and functional capacity limit causal interpretation; the results do not establish that increasing MDAR would prolong life.

ABSTRACT Low‐pressure environments are common in aircraft cabins and high‐altitude operations, where reduced oxygen partial pressure alters human physiological regulation, energy metabolism, and cognitive performance. However, existing studies primarily focus on isolated physiological responses, lacking a systematic understanding of the coupling between central neural activity and peripheral physiological adaptation under short‐term hypobaric hypoxia exposure. In this study, a controlled experiment was conducted in a hypobaric chamber under three pressure conditions (101.3, 67.2, and 56.1 kPa). Multimodal data, including electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate (HR), blood oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and respiratory‐metabolic parameters, were synchronously collected to characterize human responses across pressure levels and exposure time. Results showed that decreasing pressure significantly increased metabolic demand, with HR rising by 3.7%–5.8%, SpO 2 decreasing from 98.2% to 86.5%, and respiratory rate and metabolic rate markedly elevated, indicating typical hypoxic compensation. At the neural level, EEG spectral power shifted from low‐frequency (δ and θ) to high‐frequency (α and β) bands, with enhanced activity in frontal and occipital regions, suggesting increased cognitive resource allocation. Significant correlations between EEG features and peripheral physiological indices further revealed a coordinated central–peripheral coupling mechanism. This study provides a novel integrative perspective linking environmental pressure, metabolic cost, and neural regulation, offering new insights for cabin pressure design, human performance assessment, and human–environment interaction modeling in built environments.

Traditional models of programmatic assessment are historically rooted in highly structured, linear disciplines such as medicine (Heeneman et al., 2015; Torre et al., 2021). Translating these principles to a diverse, modular Business and Economics faculty presents profound curricular, structural, and governance challenges. Business courses within Monash University operate within a flexible architecture designed to support highly personalized student pathways, where over 90% of students have unique pathways via diverse combinations of majors, minors, and electives. Consequently, units are highly interconnected—sometimes contributing to up to 20 distinct programs—so that an assessment alteration in one unit ripples across multiple independent degree structures. This structural friction is compounded by distributed governance split across separate academic departments, departmental Directors of Education (DOEs), Course Directors, and Chief Examiners. To navigate this complex landscape, the Senior Educational Designer and the Associate Dean of Learning and Teaching (ADLT) collaborated on a university-wide initiative entitled Programmatic Assessment and Artificial Intelligence Review (PAAIR) spurred by TEQSA requirements (Lodge et al., 2023). We adapted established theory around programmatic assessment to synthesize a tailored five-principle framework, designating “Collaborative and Transparent Culture” as Principle 1. To address modular friction, we drew on Dawson’s (2020) concept of programmatic assessment security, shifting the unit of analysis from hardening every individual, isolated module to strategically securing key programmatic assessment moments across the entire course. Cultivating this shared-accountability mindset was critical because curriculum reviews occurred by course, where a single unit could feed into multiple programs with diverse departmental oversight. It was difficult to have a unified, static “full picture” of a complete course at any one stage of a review, as some units may have been completed as part of other reviews, or they may be dual-coded with a postgraduate course, requiring complex cross-referencing across courses, departments, year levels, and campuses. To bridge this diagnostic gap, we collaborated with the faculty’s data analytics team to develop the PAAIR Dashboard in PowerBI. Serving as an interactive visual analytics platform, the dashboard empowers DOEs, Course Leaders, and Educational Designers to see beyond disciplinary silos, map competency coverage across shared pathways, monitor assessment distributions, and facilitate data-informed co-design conversations in real time. It helps flag structural gaps—such as when a core graduate competency is not assessed under secure conditions at least twice per year level—ensuring curriculum resilience across highly complex student pathways. At the launch of the project, we developed a comprehensive suite of guidelines to support Unit Learning Outcome (ULO) refinement, Course Learning Outcome (CLO) mapping, and balanced assessment design. These guidelines have been instrumental in improving our course designs by scaffolding competencies progressively and designing assessment tasks with and without generative AI (Lodge et al., 2023; Matheis & John, 2024). This dual approach balances the educative, values-driven framework of academic integrity with the adversarial, hardening requirements of assessment security (Dawson, 2020). As the initiative now enters the initial transition to Business-As-Usual (BAU) operations, we are actively developing a future governance strategy to manage subsequent curriculum changes sustainably. This Pecha Kucha presentation delivers a transparent roadmap and strategic recommendations for other modular higher education faculties seeking to operationalize programmatic assessment and AI review within highly complex, non-linear educational ecosystems.

This poster presents a developing AI-enhanced polylogue methodology and conceptual framing to understand how third-space professionals in higher education are negotiating their shifting roles and identities while designing human-centred learning and assessment. Recent technological disruptions (e.g., widespread proliferation, advancement and use of generative AI, focus on cybersecurity, adoption of data-enabled technologies and ecosystems) have intensified tensions around higher education assessment structures and practices, exposing the limitations of isolated, task-based evaluation of student learning (Boud et al., 2020; Corbin et al., 2025). In response to the challenges posed to learning and assessment in the contemporary higher education landscape, emerging scholarship has foregrounded relationality and human connection alongside a shift to more program-wide approaches to assessment and assurance of learning (Lodge et al., 2023; Nicola-Richmond et al., 2025). This has highlighted questions about how educators can sustain meaningful relationships with each other and with students amidst these disruptions (Maldon et al., 2025). In this work-in-progress project, we focus on these relational questions and explore how technological disruptions are reshaping the roles and identities of educators, specifically curriculum designers working in third-space roles at the boundary of academic and professional domains (Whitchurch, 2012). We build on work that positions teaching and learning as fundamentally relational, emphasising connection, trust, care, and dialogue between educators, students, and third-space professionals (Riddle & Hickey, 2023). Our aim is to understand how relationality may be conceptualised in the context of transforming curriculum to support human flourishing and critical engagement with generative AI in our everyday learning design practice, particularly in the design of program-level assessment, feedback, mentorship, and collaborative sense-making structures. The project employs an AI-enhanced polylogue methodology inspired by Markauskaite et al. (2022). The AI-enhanced polylogue is a structured, multi-voiced inquiry, where participants engage in iterative cycles of individual reflection and collaborative dialogue, involving AI as a reflective interlocutor to surface gaps, alternative perspectives, and assumptions. Over several months, three curriculum designers independently responded to targeted questions in reflective logbooks, then engaged in semi-structured conversations about connection in higher education, program-level learning design, evolving educator roles, and the contributions of third-space professionals. This was complemented by a collaborative chat with a generative AI tool, in which participants used AI to probe gaps, tensions, and alternative perspectives arising from the conversations. These strands are then brought together in collaborative critical reflection sessions to identify emerging patterns in relational practice and their significance in program-level curriculum design. This poster shares early themes from the logbooks and conversations. Early analysis highlights how participants experience and navigate tensions between increasing technological mediation alongside their third-space roles and their commitment to relational practice. The importance of human-centred learning design and its implications will also be examined and shared. The project contributes to contemporary discussions on inter-collegial practices that keep connection, trust, and dialogue central in increasingly AI-mediated educational environments. As part of this project, participants treat disruption as an invitation to remake educator identities and practices in more relational, collaborative, and inclusive ways.

Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.

Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

Solar energy provides a promising and easily accessible renewable energy source when it comes to solving energy issues. Industries consume high amounts of energy for various uses. Thus, the concept of a solar absorber that absorbs wideband radiation is shown in this study. The absorber's configuration is MXene-Magnesium Fluoride-MXene. These structures create a novel geometry that traps the heat and absorbs a high amount of radiation. The proposed absorber's resonator layer geometry has a T-shape with a Nanodisk MXene-based resonator Solar Absorber, whose structure makes it polarization-insensitive. An average of 95.57% absorption was achieved within the range of 200-3000 nm, keeping absorptance above 96% over a bandwidth nm while exceeding 92% over a much wider bandwidth of around 2120 nm across the spectral spectrum under investigation. Moreover, this suggested absorber achieved 94.9% average absorption under AM 1.5. Examined several solar absorber structures and the findings. Optimized the design over several parameters and examined the outcome. Then, analyzed the Transverse Electric and magnetic fields with magnetic and electric colour-changing fields, which are described in the results section. The research presents clear engineering outcomes for solar thermal absorber design, with machine learning methods demonstrating the application of artificial intelligence in the study. The examination shows that the Machine Learning model's maximum achievable R 2 value of 0.93 for parameter change intends to minimize the simulation period by a quarter when compared with older methods, while minimizing other simulation needs. The high absorption rate with a unique resonator design is promising for applications as a renewable solar dryer for mining.

Abstract Purpose To compare the reading level of paediatric health guidance, parents' own questions and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot responses to those questions, and to test whether chatbots adapt to the reading level of the person asking. Methods Cross-sectional study, reported following the Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool (CHART), of 18,392 guideline pages (17,516 family-facing, 876 clinician-facing) from 86 organisations, 1,000 parent-authored questions sampled from 23,477 public forum posts, and 5,000 responses to those questions from five commercially deployed chatbots. Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) was the primary outcome, with six secondary metrics. In a sub-study, 100 questions were resubmitted with an instruction to match the reader's level or to answer at sixth-grade level (1,500 responses). Results Median FKGL was 12.51 for clinician-facing guidance, 9.08 for family-facing guidance, 8.37 for chatbot responses and 6.15 for parents' questions. The American Medical Association sixth-grade standard was exceeded by 99.3% of clinician-facing pages, 92.6% of family-facing pages and 89.2% of chatbot responses. Every chatbot answered above the reading level of the question asked (median difference + 1.21 to + 3.57 grades). Given an explicit sixth-grade instruction, the median gap narrowed in every model and three of five answered below the reader's level. Conclusion Paediatric health information from institutions and chatbots alike is written above the level of its readers. Chatbots do not adapt to the reader by default, but can when instructed.

documents.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

Abstract The stress of work is a significant issue in the occupational health arena for college students because of the uncertainty of employment, evolving labor market expectations and preparation for the world of work. The existing methods are mainly based on psychological assessment instead of intelligent adjustment of stress according to the occupational health. This study is to design an Adaptive Vortex Optimizer (AVO) based Attention-Based Dueling Deep Q-Network (AD-DQN) model for intelligent adjustment of college students'' employment stress based on personalized decision optimization. The Occupational Employment Stress dataset consists of 15,000 student responses from multiple data sources, including university career guidance, health questionnaires, academic profiles, internship experiences, and students'' self-reported stress responses. Imputation using the K-Nearest Neighbor, Min–Max normalization and outlier refinement are used to enhance data quality. Deep Autoencoder-based feature extraction aims to obtain compact representation by capturing salient occupational, behavioral and educational traits and removing redundant information. The proposed model is designed to use extracted features to optimize the learning parameters and exploration strategies using AVO for efficient convergence. An Attention Mechanism (AM) selects important occupational health and employment related stress signals whereas a Dueling DQN is used to construct an intervention policy for an individual by estimating state value and action advantage. Feedback is offered and the RL constantly adjusts recommendations, thereby furthering career readiness and stress regulation. Experiments conducted in Python show superior performance in terms of 0.982 Accuracy, 0.963 Recall, 0.97 AUC, 0.94 F1-Score and 0.91 Kappa when compared to existing models. From these results, the classification reliability and discriminative ability have been improved, balanced prediction performance and consistent decision making have been achieved. AVO-AD-DQN can support university career-counseling services by enabling personalized employment-stress assessment and adaptive stress-management recommendations.

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Marketing technology (MarTech) education has traditionally emphasised the acquisition of discrete platform skills, often resulting in fragmented, “tool-first” approaches that inadequately prepare graduates to manage complex MarTech ecosystems. At the same time, the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified concerns about whether conventional assessment designs can validly evaluate higher-order capabilities such as judgement, strategic reasoning, and decision making (Corbin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024). These converging challenges highlight an urgent need for Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) innovations grounded in human-centred design that foster systems thinking and strategic decision making while providing authentic, AI-resilient assessment opportunities. This presentation introduces Orchestrate, a low-fidelity (LoFi) MarTech simulation designed to cultivate systems thinking and assess industry-ready capability development in undergraduate and postgraduate marketing programs. Developed in Microsoft Excel, a widely available and low-barrier technology, the simulation provides a scalable and accessible learning experience. Informed by industry practice, Orchestrate positions students as marketing leaders responsible for managing investments across an interconnected MarTech ecosystem. Piloted during Semester 1, 2026, with Bachelor of Commerce students undertaking the Marketing Technology major at RMIT University, student teams balanced competing priorities to optimise customer acquisition, retention, satisfaction, and revenue growth. Rather than learning isolated technologies, students allocated finite budgets across 12 capability areas aligned to the People, Process, Data, and Technology (PPDT) framework (Monshizada et al., 2023). The pedagogical design is underpinned by systems thinking theory, which emphasises understanding interdependencies, trade-offs, and emergent patterns within complex systems (York et al., 2019). The simulation makes relationships between MarTech capabilities explicit, demonstrating that sustainable organisational performance emerges from balancing people, process, data, and technological priorities rather than investing in individual tools. Authentic assessment principles further situate learning within realistic professional contexts that mirror contemporary marketing practice. A distinctive contribution of Orchestrate lies in its AI-resilient assessment design. Rather than relying on static written outputs that can readily be generated or enhanced by GenAI, assessment focuses on students’ situated decision making within the dynamic simulation environment. Teams must justify their evolving strategies, explain the consequences of their choices, and demonstrate alignment between investment decisions, course principles, and organisational performance outcomes. Because gameplay produces different conditions and outcomes for each team, the design reduces opportunities for inappropriate AI assistance while maintaining a focus on higher-order judgement and strategic reasoning. Early evidence from the Semester 1, 2026 pilot indicates strong student engagement and learning. Assessment submissions demonstrated sustained engagement with the simulation, while reflective responses showed strong understanding of course concepts and application of relevant theoretical frameworks to strategic decisions. Qualitative student experience survey feedback also identified Orchestrate as a key highlight of the course. These findings are indicative rather than the result of a formal research evaluation; a comprehensive Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) study is now being developed, with an ethics application underway, to investigate the simulation’s impact on systems thinking, strategic decision making, student engagement, and learning outcomes.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Positioned at the intersection of pedagogy, technology, and curriculum design, learning designers play an increasingly important role in the design, development, and enhancement of learning experiences across diverse educational contexts. Their work has been described as being characterised by collaboration, relationship-building, and the ability to facilitate change within complex educational environments (Altena et al. 2025; Walji, 2023). Recent research further suggests that effective learning design depends on adaptive relational work, trust, openness, and the integration of diverse forms of expertise across interdisciplinary teams (Papageorgiou & Bennett, 2026). Existing studies have explored learning designers’ demographic profiles, qualifications, professional backgrounds, career pathways, job titles, and professional positioning, particularly within higher education (Altena et al., 2025; Gilmore & Nguyen, 2023; Mitchell et al., 2017; Slade et al., 2019). Learning designers have also been conceptualised as “third-space” or hybrid professionals whose work spans pedagogical, technological, and organisational boundaries (Bennett, 2023; Whitchurch, 2012), and competency frameworks have been proposed to describe their professional capabilities (MacLean & Scott, 2011; Simpson, 2025). However, there remains limited evidence about learning designers working outside higher education and little empirical research examining how learning designers themselves perceive the knowledge, skills, and values that underpin successful professional practice. This presentation reports preliminary findings from a larger survey of 268 learning designers working in Australia (88%) and New Zealand (5%) across diverse contexts, including formal education (K–12 and tertiary), enterprise, government, and not-for-profit organisations. The presentation focuses on respondents’ perceptions of the knowledge, skills, and values that constitute the “special sauce” of learning design practice. Data was collected through a cross-sectional online survey and participation was on a voluntary basis. The findings suggest that learning designers perceive the human-centred dimensions of their work as more central to their professional practice than the technical dimensions commonly associated with the role. Collaboration with subject matter experts was the most frequently reported task performed by learning designers and interpersonal skills were the most frequently selected skill, highlighting the collaborative and relational nature of the role. A high proportion of respondents identified knowledge of learning and motivation theories as a core knowledge domain underpinning effective learning design practice, followed by knowledge of educational technologies and digital learning environments. Strong emphasis was also placed on proficiency with learning management systems as an essential skill. The values identified by respondents further suggest the profession’s strong orientation toward critical thinking, empathy, and adaptability. While technological knowledge and skills were widely recognised as important, particularly educational technology and digital learning environments, and learning management systems, they were identified slightly less frequently than the human-centred aspects of the role. These findings suggest that, although technology is an important component of learning design practice, practitioners primarily appear to prioritise collaboration, learner support, and the application of human judgement as essential to the role rather than technological expertise alone. The presentation concludes by arguing that, as artificial intelligence and automation increasingly undertake routine technical and production tasks, the future value of learning designers may lie less in the technologies they can use and more in their uniquely human capabilities, including empathy, communication, collaboration, critical judgement, and the ability to bring people together around better learning experiences. In this sense, the “special sauce” of learning design practice may not be technological expertise but people skills. Moving the field forward will therefore require a stronger sociological and philosophical foundation for understanding how these human capabilities can be developed, valued, and sustained as educational technologies continue to evolve.

Background. Personal autonomy represents one of the key competencies of modern education, playing a decisive role in the development of intrinsic motivation, responsibility, and students’ active involvement in the educational process.
