In fact, scholars have begun to recognise that current writing practices resulting in hybrid texts co-constructed by humans and AI are making it difficult, if not impossible, to identify distinct boundaries between AI-generated output and a student’s own intellectual efforts (e.g. Eaton, 2023; Wu et al., 2026). Higher education is in a season where excitement, curiosity, and unease about generative AI’s impact on academic work and learning sit in tension. Even as one who has actively sought to engage students in discussions of how we can productively and legitimately use generative AI in our writing, I found myself having unexpected reactions (of relief) when I encountered assignments with linguistic infelicities of the sort that suggested their writers had not used generative AI. The way forward, this presentation suggests, requires an intentional commitment to prioritise pedagogical approaches that foreground human connection – both in terms of cultivating a renewed intellectual and emotional connection of students with their own work, and in terms of building connection between students and instructors through open dialogue and compassionate, nuanced approaches to teaching and assessing.

The arrival of capable generative AI (GenAI) tools has posed a genuine and largely unresolved challenge for summative assessment in higher education. When AI-generated submissions evade institutional detection 94% of the time and examination scores rise sharply without any change in teaching, the evidentiary basis of take-home and invigilated assessment is genuinely in question. This paper draws on two lines of work to argue that classroom-based gamified problem-based formative assessment (GPBFA) offers a more durable response than detection-focused approaches. The first line is an empirical study of saval.app, a GPBFA platform evaluated through Keller’s ARCS motivational model across a full university semester (pre n = 41, post n = 44). Results across all four ARCS dimensions were encouraging (all p < .0001; Cronbach’s alpha > .93; composite 81% positive response rate), with near-zero motivational decline across 12 weeks. The second line is a review of UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Frameworks for Teachers and Students, which we argue are philosophically and pedagogically aligned with classroom GPBFA in ways the existing literature has not yet made explicit. Taken together, we suggest that moving assessment into the classroom — where it is live, observed, and problem-centred — may address both the integrity challenge and the AI literacy imperative that UNESCO frameworks define.

Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

This article examines the application of gamification in literature education as a means of increasing students' motivation and engagement. It analyses the theoretical foundations of gamification, including self-determination theory and game-based learning principles, and describes a quasi-experimental study in which game elements such as points, levels, badges, quests and narrative roles were integrated into literature lessons. The findings indicate that a carefully designed gamified environment strengthens intrinsic motivation, encourages regular reading, improves participation in discussions and deepens students' interpretation of literary texts.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Australian higher education has responded to generative artificial intelligence with an ambitious program of assessment reform. Structural approaches, most visibly the two-lane model, seek to sustain trust in degrees by securing some assessments while opening others to AI partnership. This conceptual paper argues that the reform consensus, now sharpened by sector attention to assurance of learning and adaptive capabilities, addresses validity more directly than formation. Assessment tasks are not only measurement occasions; they can also be sites of the cognitive work through which capability develops. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship, desirable difficulties and cognitive offloading, the paper introduces the apprenticeship layer: the stratum of entry-level cognitive work through which expertise has historically been developed and renewed. As AI is increasingly used to perform parts of this work in workplaces and universities, institutions face a risk of certifying capabilities without reliably preserving the practice through which those capabilities are formed. The paper proposes three principles for formation-centred design: friction by design, process as both learning and evidence, and a care floor of guaranteed human attention. It concludes that valid judgement and capability formation are different questions that assessment can and should be designed to answer together.

Designing an undergraduate systems thinking course in 2023 took months. Workshops, whiteboards, an academic drafting offline, iteration, constructive alignment, compliance, and endless box-moving on a digital canvas. One decision shaped the course: the learning designer judged 10 assessment submission points across 12 weeks excessive and argued to reduce them. The academic, who had taught the discipline for years, refused. Systems thinking concepts interlock, and a student who has not grasped one cannot proceed. The checkpoints were not overload; they were scaffolding. The design bent to the discipline, and the disciplinary expert was right. Generative AI could now compress much of that. It can propose a structure, recommend staggered low-stakes checkpoints for interdependent concepts, and draft the content beneath them. It might well have reached that assessment design faster. Learning designers are tempted to insist something irreplaceable is lost. Much of it is not: a considerable portion of that time was drag, and automating drag is a good outcome. The argument here is not that slowness was valuable. What mattered was less visible. Working on unfamiliar material, the learning designer frequently does not understand the subject. This is usually treated as a limitation. It is better understood as an instrument. The designer is an authentic novice, and their confusion is diagnostic: when an explanation fails for them, it will fail for a student (Wieman, 2007). This is the logic of usability testing: a designer cannot test an interface they already know (Nielsen, 1993). A language model can usefully simulate a novice reader. What it cannot replace is genuine uncertainty: having absorbed the discipline, it fills gaps silently rather than experiencing them. But the instrument only works under a particular social condition. To say “I do not understand this” to an academic, repeatedly, about their own subject, requires standing, which no third space role description confers (Whitchurch, 2008). It is built through months of meetings, shared frustration, and accumulated trust, and it is what made the academic willing to re-explain rather than dismiss. The re-explanation is where the design insight came from. This is the uncomfortable possibility. The inefficiency was not valuable in itself, but the relationship formed inside it, and the relationship is the precondition for the human contribution. Compress the process into an afternoon and the drag disappears, along with the conditions in which trust is made. We have no way to tell which parts of a slow process were waste and which were connection. This Pecha Kucha presents a real course design, concedes what AI could do faster, and identifies what it cannot replace: genuine uncertainty, professional judgement, and trust. For institutions adopting AI-supported workflows, the practical implication is to protect time for co-design and explanation, treating relationship-building as work rather than overhead. It closes with a question beneath the debates about AI and the third space workforce (Bearman et al., 2023; Huijser et al., 2024): if the relationship was produced by the inefficiency we are now eliminating, can human-centred design survive its own optimisation?

Purpose This study examines how value is co-created and how trust and coordination are institutionally sustained in a peer-to-peer (P2P) service in which monetary exchange is prohibited at the operational core. Service-dominant (S-D) logic has increasingly theorised value co-creation as coordinated by institutional arrangements within service ecosystems, yet the institutional arrangements it has examined are overwhelmingly market-based. Taking World Wide Opportunities on Organic Farms (WWOOF) as a critical case, the study develops the concept of the decommodification paradox: the co-existence of a non-monetary dyadic exchange with monetary elements at adjacent layers of the service ecosystem, sustained through participants' ongoing institutional work. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative, interpretivist design was adopted. Twenty semi-structured interviews with WWOOF hosts and WWOOFers across 6 Indian states, purposively sampled, were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Findings Four themes were generated: (1) value as co-produced labour, learning and dwelling; (2) trust sustained through values-based self-selection, small-community reputation and refusal rather than algorithmic verification; (3) the decommodification paradox, in which the non-monetary dyad is preserved by participants' work of placing monetary elements at the platform and peripheral layers and (4) dark-side dynamics of asymmetry, isolation and gendered labour, read as value co-destruction at the interfaces between layers, that mark the arrangement's boundary conditions. Originality/value The study reframes decommodification in P2P services as a layered property of a service ecosystem rather than a binary attribute of an institution, extends the institutional turn in S-D logic to non-market coordination, identifies the practices that maintain such arrangements and positions the paradox against hybrid-economy, pseudo-sharing and value co-destruction perspectives.

This study examines the role of psychology in sports performance, with a particular focus on tennis, an individual sport characterized by intense mental pressure and constant self-regulation. Since psychology became a modern science through the work of Wilhelm Wundt, researchers have explored how thoughts, emotions, and behavior influence human performance. In tennis, psychological factors often determine the difference between an ordinary player and a champion. Based on Pierre Janet’s concept of “conduct,” every action, reaction, and decision made by a tennis player represents an attempt to adapt to competitive situations and manage internal tension. The paper highlights the importance of sensory-perceptive processes in tennis performance. Ordinary players generally display synthetic perception, meaning they are easily distracted by external factors such as crowd noise, weather conditions, or previous mistakes. They often attribute errors to external causes rather than analyzing their own actions. In contrast, champions demonstrate analytical perception, allowing them to focus selectively on relevant details, such as ball speed, body positioning,and the opponent’s movements. Champions also possess advanced mental representation abilities, enabling them to anticipate future actions and strategically plan points before they begin. Another major aspect discussed is stress and emotional regulation. For ordinary players, stress produces emotional instability, muscular tension, and chaotic thinking, all of which negatively affect technicalexecution and decision-making. Champions, however, are capable of transforming negative emotions such as fear or frustration into motivation and determination. Their ability to quickly forget mistakes and refocus on the next point is essential for maintaining performance under stress. Finally, the paper proposes practical psychological strategies for stress management and performanceimprovement, including positive self-talk, motor skill automation, controlled body language, and concentration rituals. The conclusion emphasizes that mastering psychological processes is fundamental for achieving excellence in tennis and transforming talent into championship-level performance.

Emotional experiences are fundamental inputs to human development, yet we know surprisingly little about their distribution in everyday life. Research typically characterizes children’s emotional environments using global reports or brief observations, obscuring the real-time contexts in which emotions arise. Here, we used artificial intelligence to automatically transcribe and annotate daylong audio recordings from three samples totaling N=159 families with children aged 5 months-8 years old (48.43% female). Our findings reveal the architecture of children’s everyday emotional environments: positive speech was concentrated during play and music, and 25% of speech segments conveyed frustration, concentrated during routine caregiving. Mothers’ mental health did not predict affective speech, but lower child effortful control predicted more frustration in our toddler sample. Frustration peaked in early toddlerhood, suggesting that children’s growing independence at this age may reorganize family emotional environments. Overall, emotional speech appears to emerge from everyday activity, with meaningful shifts across development.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

documents.abstract: Soil health is essential for sustainable agricultural development, and soil microorganisms play an indispensable role in maintaining and improving it. Soil microbial communities influence soil’s physical, chemical, and biological properties through multiple pathways, including promoting nutrient cycling, improving soil structure, decomposing pollutants, and providing biological control against pathogens and pests. This paper comprehensively reviews the complex relationships between soil microorganisms and soil health, focusing on the key mechanisms by which microbial communities contribute to soil health enhancement. It also analyzes the effects of environmental and human factors on microbial community structure and function. In addition, the study discusses the specific applications of soil microorganisms in agriculture, particularly in bioremediation, microbial fertilizers, and biocontrol agent development. This study aims to reveal how soil microorganisms impact soil health, assess their potential applications in agricultural management, and provide scientific support for sustainable agricultural development and soil resource conservation.

Learning design is increasingly central to higher education, yet practitioners continue to grapple with questions of identity, recognition and collective purpose. Building on previous ASCILITE conversations about professional standards for learning design, this working symposium builds upon previous symposia on this theme to move from questions about what learning designers do to what learning design stands for. Participants will be invited to co-author draft principles for a Learning Design Manifesto, articulating the values, commitments and purposes that should guide the field in a period shaped by generative AI, institutional reform, hybrid education and demands for scalability. Through short provocations based on existing research, guided group work and live synthesis, participants will develop, test and prioritise candidate principles.

Generative AI has pushed universities to review curriculum at pace and scale, raising urgent questions about assessment, academic integrity and graduate capability. At Monash University, the Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project required faculties to examine assessment and AI integration at program level. This paper asks how educational designers can support teaching teams to make program-level curriculum decisions while AI practice, policy and disciplinary expectations are still unsettled. We use a practice-based reflective case study methodology across the faculties of Science, Arts and Information Technology. Data sources include workshop designs, curriculum artefacts, participant feedback, program mapping outputs and facilitator reflection. Our analysis examines how Kaospilot methods, including vision backcasting, shared canvases and visible artefacts, created structured conditions for teaching teams to work with uncertainty, surface disciplinary values and make program-scale thinking visible. The cases show both the promise and constraint of adapting Kaospilot methods to faculty-wide change. The method helped create the human conditions for programmatic AI review, but its impact depended on artefacts, documentation, leadership, governance pathways and continuing educational design work. The paper argues that AI curriculum review requires structured social conditions to enact policy settings.

Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.

Maintaining academic integrity is a serious issue in higher education, affecting the paradigms governing the production and dissemination of human knowledge. Although a significant body of research has explored the ethics of AI tool usage in higher education settings, these studies have neglected to examine the power relations inherent within them. In response to this issue, this study employs Bourdieu’s theories of symbolic violence and actor-network theory to review the AI usage policies of Australian higher education institutions and mainstream academic journal publishers. Specifically, actor-network theory is first applied to identify the governance networks surrounding AI usage within the technological adoption process, thereby establishing that AI tools act as mediating agents that actively facilitate communication between institutions and users. Furthermore, symbolic violence provides a comprehensive explanation of the means by which power-holding institutions legitimise such governance. In summary, the aim of this inquiry is to expose and challenge the “false pretences” of AI ethics regulations that merely adjust, reinforce and gloss over the status quo, thereby channelling the potential of AI towards justice and combating latent human bias. documents.abstract: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making. However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity. In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI. We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995). The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Anxiety and depressive disorders affect over 500 million people globally, with a treatment gap exceeding 75% in low- and middle-income countries. Current diagnostic frameworks rely on clinical interview and self-report, with test–retest reliability of 0.20 to 0.67 for these disorders in DSM-5 field trials. Autonomic nervous system dysregulation is a well-established biological correlate of anxiety and depression. We report the first, to our knowledge, prospective clinical validation of an autonomic biomarker-based artificial intelligence system against a blinded psychiatrist reference standard in routine clinical practice. Methods We conducted a prospective, two-site diagnostic accuracy study at tertiary hospitals in Delhi and Kerala, India (CTRI/2023/07/054984). The Xaant Resting Autonomic Signature (X-RAS) platform, a three-layer LSTM with self-attention previously developed on an independent cohort of 2,349 participants and frozen prior to the trial, analysed electrodermal activity and blood volume pulse from 15-minute resting-state recordings and produced a four-class diagnostic classification. Of 180 participants enrolled, 170 completed the protocol. Out of these, 114 clinical participants with DSM-5 depression, anxiety, or comorbid disorders, and 56 reference group participants recruited from a long-term meditation practice tradition were considered. The reference standard was the DSM-5 diagnosis established by the site psychiatrist, who was blinded to the platform output. The primary outcome was Cohen's kappa for AI-psychiatrist diagnostic agreement within the clinical cohort. Results Within the clinical cohort, the platform achieved 93.0% agreement with clinical diagnosis (κ = 0.884, 95% CI 0.789 to 0.956), with 100% sensitivity for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) detection in the GAD subgroup (n = 15, 95% CI 78.2 to 100). All eight classification disagreements fell along the depression–comorbid boundary, and the AI classification agreed with the patient's own self-categorisation in five of the eight. Performance was consistent across the two sites (Delhi 94.6%, Kerala 91.4%, p = 0.527) and across age, sex, and education subgroups. Classical autonomic markers separated the clinical and reference groups with moderate to large effect sizes (d = 0.53 to 0.84). Two of the physiological constructs of the development-cohort, namely Hypoactivity and Experience, were reproduced at the group level in independently diagnosed patients. A per-minute slope analysis of the tonic EDA signal showed a transdiagnostic reversal, where the baseline settled downward during rest in the reference group and drifted upward across all three clinical subgroups (Kruskal–Wallis p = 3.0 × 10⁻²²). Conclusions Resting-state autonomic AI analysis provides objective diagnostic support for anxiety and depressive disorders, with Cohen’s κ = 0.884 (95% CI 0.789 to 0.956) against psychiatrist-assigned DSM-5 diagnoses in routine outpatient practice. Direct comparison with published inter-rater or test-retest reliability estimates is not appropriate given differences in methodology and reference standards. The platform's low cost, portability, and suitability for non-specialist operators support scalability in resource-limited settings. External validation in primary care, community, telehealth, and non-Indian populations is the next step for the programme. Trial registration: Clinical Trials Registry of India, CTRI/2023/07/054984, registered July 2023.

documents.abstract: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

The growing interest in eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has stimulated research on models with built-in interpretability, among which part-prototype models are particularly prominent. Part-Prototype Models (PPMs) classify inputs by comparing them to learned prototypes and provide human-understandable explanations of the form “this looks like that.” Despite this intrinsic interpretability, PPMs have not yet emerged as a competitive alternative to post-hoc explanation methods. This survey reviews work published between 2019 and 2025 and derives a taxonomy of the challenges faced by current PPMs. The analysis reveals a diverse set of open problems. The main issue concerns the quality and number of learned prototypes. Further challenges include limited generalization across tasks and contexts, as well as methodological shortcomings such as non-standardized evaluation. Five broad research directions are identified: improving predictive performance, developing theoretically grounded architectures, establishing frameworks for human-AI collaboration, aligning models with human concepts, and defining robust metrics and benchmarks for evaluation. The survey aims to stimulate further research and promote intrinsically interpretable models for practical applications. A curated list of the surveyed papers is available at https://github.com/aix-group/ppm-survey .

Abstract In June 2025 and February 2026, the wars involving the United States, Israel and Iran led to content about nuclear war being posted on social media, particularly on TikTok and Instagram. In this article, I ask what practices social media creators are enacting to deal with perceived nuclear danger and explore how the practices relate to the struggle for agency to participate in international politics. I utilised practice theory and digital ethnography to analyse 146 short videos, allowing me particularly to expand the relations of practice theory with visualities, the study of popular culture and world politics, sociotechnical imaginaries, and workshops as methodology. I find that practices that digital creators enact can be described as nuclear nihilism, postapocalyptic imagining, nuclear education, and social media self-reflection. While nuclear nihilism describes the tendency to approach nuclear danger with indifference rather than anxiety, postapocalyptic imaginaries are visual depictions of an often romanticised post–nuclear war landscape. Nuclear education aims to spread knowledge about nuclear weapons, and self-reflection about social media addresses the absurdity of producing videos on nuclear war at all. The role of agency is ambivalent: Whereas some creators expect to possess hegemonic agency in a postapocalyptic reality, others grieve about their missing agency regarding nuclear weapons politics and about changing life during a permacrisis at large.

We evaluated Jev, a non-generative decision model, for title and abstract screening using 4527 records from two systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments previously used in our 2024 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Human decisions to retain records for full-text assessment served as the reference. In the primary analysis, Jev answered yes-or-no questions (Noul); at a prespecified 50% cutoff, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For direct model comparison, Jev used explicit include/exclude options (Choice) and the same prompts as GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra. Jev Choice achieved sensitivity and specificity similar to or higher than those of GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra, while API charges per 1000 records were US$0.043 for Jev, US$0.57 for GPT-5 mini, and US$7.39 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev retained all reports ultimately included in both reviews across all tested conditions and runs. Although these findings do not establish that decision models can replace human reviewers, they support Jev as a promising, low-cost alternative to the tested generative LLM configurations for assisting human title and abstract screening. Independent validation across diverse review topics is needed to assess Jev’s generalizability and utility in human-supervised screening workflows.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The article presents an overview of the scientific biography and major achievements of Alexander Alexandrovich Oboznov, Doctor of Psychology, Professor, and one of the leading Russian specialists in the fields of work psychology, engineering psychology, and ergonomics. The article examines his contribution to developing the situational-dynamic concept of the systemic mental regulation of professional activity, as well as the concepts of situational prerequisites and unified space of mental regulation resources. The work pays particular attention to Oboznov’s development of the problem of human trust in technology, including the phenomena of overtrust and overmistrust, trust calibration, and human-operator interaction with the systems equipped with artificial intelligence elements. The connection between his research and current trends in human-machine interaction psychology is demonstrated, along with its relevance to ensure the reliability and safety of professional activity in the context of digitalization.
topics: Academic and Historical Perspectives in Psychology

documents.abstract: Background The Fishbowl is a discussion format: an inner ring discusses a prompt while an outer ring observes and swaps in (Bermudez, n.d.). When it runs well, the interaction reaches the interactive tier of Chi and Wylie’s (2014) ICAP framework, most strongly linked to deep learning. Novice teachers struggle to orchestrate so complex a discussion and often avoid it or run it as procedural theatre (Dillenbourg, 2002), while students lack the scaffolding to grasp what good discussion looks like or to notice their participation in real time. Fixed-seat rooms make the concentric-ring layout harder to set up. The shift An LMS-embedded learning tool can address these problems by scaffolding through the interface itself: built-in phase sequencing and role-specific views support teachers as drivers rather than executors (Dillenbourg, 2013), while giving students concrete moves for good discussion and cues to notice their participation. Such a tool was never technically impossible, only unjustifiable, requiring a software team and budget cycle for one learning activity. Generative AI now lets a single learning designer (LD) author and revise a version between deliveries, so refinement moves at the tempo of teaching rather than procurement. However, unmediated “vibe coding” is fragile across accessibility, security, and pedagogical validity. Vibe engineering (Willison, 2025) is the discipline that makes the speed safe. Development snapshot Vibe engineering can be brought to education by drawing on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) orchestration and collaboration-script theory (Fischer et al., 2013; Kollar et al., 2006): balancing under- and over-scripting (Dillenbourg, 2002), preserving intrinsic script constraints (Dillenbourg & Tchounikine, 2007), and scaffolding transactive discourse (Fischer et al., 2013). Each version is audited in a separate AI session against accessibility and security checklists, while pedagogical validity is judged by the LD through CSCL orchestration principles and classroom observation. Every update ships as one small static HTML file, stored centrally with no student data and no runtime AI, so it propagates automatically to every unit that uses it. Poster experience Live demonstration on two adjacent devices: the projected Fishbowl discussion phase (teacher-facing) alongside the private ideas phase (student-facing). Annotated walkthrough of core design elements with their theoretical warrants. A few major versions showing how the tool evolved, with a QR link to selected prompt history. The accessibility and security checklists, with a QR link to the open-source versions. Relevance to the theme: Human-centred learning design The Fishbowl builds connection through structured dialogue, and the tool preserves that priority. It orchestrates the room without mediating the conversation, and the interface directs student attention to peers rather than screens. The approach is not specific to one activity: in principle, any collaboration script an LD can specify pedagogically could be authored at teaching tempo (cf. Holstein et al., 2019). Next steps The tool will run across teaching periods in 2026, with observations of orchestration load, participation, and facilitator experience feeding back into design rationales, checklists, and successive versions. The two checklists will be released as open-source, citable Markdown artefacts for the LD community.

This exploratory study examines how collaboration structures and engagement processes are associated with interdisciplinary knowledge construction among pre-service professionals engaged in AI-focused instructional design. There is not enough empirical evidence about professional collaboration when designing AI-integrated supports for diverse learners (Martinez-Maldonado et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2021). Little is known about how participation structures relate to the depth of cognitive engagement and knowledge integration that emerges during that process. This study used an exploratory, process-oriented discourse analysis that combined qualitative turn-level coding with descriptive frequencies. The researchers analyzed video-recorded collaborative discourse among pre-service special education teachers and pre-service school psychologists (N = 14) from an interdisciplinary graduate seminar focused on AI-integrated instructional design. The analysis used turn-level coding of participation patterns, cognitive and metacognitive engagement, and activation of an expanded Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. The expanded framework incorporates Psychological Knowledge (PsychK) and Interdisciplinary Knowledge (IK). The study examined 3111 analytic turns across three interdisciplinary groups. It explored how participation distribution and cross-disciplinary exchange related to epistemic depth during collaboration. Groups with more distributed participation and more cross-disciplinary interaction tended to engage more often in high-level cognitive and metacognitive processes. They also showed broader combined activation of PsychK and IK related to AI tool use, learner variability, and ethical considerations. Groups with more concentrated participation tended toward procedural or discipline-specific reasoning, with limited activation of PsychK and IK. These patterns suggest that collaboration structure may play a role in shaping the kinds of professional knowledge that become salient during AI-focused interdisciplinary work. The study involved three groups in one seminar, its patterns describe these groups and should not be generalized. Group composition by discipline is a plausible alternative explanation for some of them. This exploratory study conceptualized interdisciplinary collaboration as an epistemic practice. It offered empirical insight into how professional knowledge may be negotiated under conditions of AI-mediated educational change. It proposed the epistemic ceiling as an exploratory theoretical proposition for future testing. The findings have implications for interdisciplinary educator preparation programs that aim to support ethical and inclusive AI integration as a collective, relational process. Future research with larger and more diverse samples could examine whether these patterns generalize across institutional and professional contexts.

Artificial Neural Networks, the building blocks of AI, were inspired by the human brain’s network of neurons. Over the years, these networks have evolved to replicate complex capabilities of the brain, allowing them to handle tasks such as image and language processing. In the realm of Large Language Models, there has been a keen interest in making the language learning process more akin to that of humans. Motivated by neuroscience research that has shown that different grammatical categories are processed by different neurons in the brain, we show that LLMs operate in a similar way. Utilizing Llama 3 and Qwen2, we identify the most important neurons associated with the prediction of words belonging to different part-of-speech tags. Using the achieved knowledge, we train a classifier on a dataset, which shows that the activation patterns of these key neurons can reliably predict part-of-speech tags on fresh data. The results suggest that LLMs develop specialized neural representations for capturing part-of-speech tag concepts.

Women remain underrepresented in cybersecurity higher education and the workforce, with participation and retention influenced by confidence, belonging, professional identity, mentoring, and career readiness. While Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly supporting technical learning in cybersecurity, its potential to enhance students’ broader development remains underexplored. This conceptual position paper proposes a Human + Agentic AI mentoring ecosystem in which Agentic AI mentors complement, rather than replace, human mentors, educators, peers, and professional communities. Integrating Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), women in cybersecurity literature, and human-centred AI design, we present a conceptual framework and design implications for Agentic AI mentoring that supports confidence, belonging, professional identity, career readiness and workforce transition. The framework extends AI beyond technical tutoring towards human-centred, co-designed mentoring across academic, social, and professional dimensions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract Maritime transportation is the backbone of global trade, yet it faces significant fire safety challenges, particularly in cargo handling. Fires on container ships account for 55% of all maritime fire incidents, with 92.6% originating from cargo, often involving misdeclared dangerous goods (DG). These fires lead to catastrophic consequences, including vessel damage, container loss, and environmental pollution. The OVERHEAT EU-funded Horizon project introduces a cutting-edge Digital Solution (DS) designed to enhance operational efficiency and maritime fire safety through synchronized offshore-onshore DS enabling real-time collaboration between ship crews, port authorities, and emergency responders, providing a unified and real-time view of unfolding emergencies. The architecture leverages IoT-enabled sensors, UAV-assisted thermal imaging, and AI-powered decision support tools to detect and assess fire hazards with high accuracy and speed. This integrated awareness significantly enhances the Shared Situational Awareness (SSA) resulting in coordinated decision-making, reduced response times, which in effect improves the effectiveness of mitigation efforts. Beyond technological innovation, the OVERHEAT project also emphasizes the importance of fostering a proactive safety culture (SC). This paper presents the challenges in maritime firefighting, the design and implementation of OVERHEAT’s DS, discusses its potential for improving maritime fire safety, and outlines future validation efforts through simulation and real-world trials in European ports.

Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.

The scientific article investigates the complex problem of the formation and dynamics of motivation in the educational and professional activity of university students within the framework of ongoing educational reforms. The study aims to determine the specific psychological and pedagogical features of students’ learning motives development and to substantiate a system of effective tools, conditions, and factors for increasing their cognitive and professional activity during their university studies. A complex of scientific methods was applied, including a systematic theoretical analysis of psychological literature and an empirical research project (surveying and diagnosing) involving approximately 300 1st, 2nd, and 4th-year students of Vinnytsia Mykhailo Kotsiubynskyi State Pedagogical University, alongside university professors. The findings revealed a highly contradictory dynamics of the motivational sphere across different years of study. While the majority of students maintain a responsible attitude toward their education, the direct cognitive interest, internal learning drive, and emotional satisfaction from the process significantly decrease from junior to senior courses. This drop in intrinsic motivation is gradually replaced by purely pragmatic and formal factors, such as the necessity of passing exams, external attendance control, and future career competitiveness. Based on the results, the key conditions for fostering sustainable intrinsic motivation were highlighted: ensuring intellectual independence, creating problem-based situations, offering a differentiated task system, encouraging freedom of choice, and implementing innovative teaching approaches. The practical value of the work lies in proposing over twenty specific interactive methods to enhance students’ motivational sphere through optimized teacher-student partnership.

Learning designers (LDs) play a critical role in supporting higher education teaching and learning, especially through periods of significant digital change, from the rapid transition to online learning during COVID-19 to the redesign of learning and assessment in response to generative AI. In this increasingly digital and AI-enabled higher education sector, learning design is inherently relational, requiring practitioners to meet academics where they are and support educational change through trust, collaboration and compassion. Yet much of this work remains hidden, and difficult to articulate and demonstrate using traditional institutional measures. While output metrics such as consultations, workshops and resources developed provide evidence of activity, they often fail to capture the relational, collaborative and transformative nature of LD practice. Drawing on King and Patterson’s (2026) conception of course design as an act of care, we argue that many of the most significant contributions of LDs are relational rather than transactional. To address this challenge Boreland et al. (2025) developed the Learning Design Evidence Framework (LDEF) which provides a structured approach to evidencing the relational work underpinning educational innovation. The framework makes visible how LDs build trust, foster collaboration, influence practice, and create the conditions for meaningful educational change using seven segments; Student-Centered Design, Curriculum Design and Innovation, Professional Development, Promotion and Sharing of Quality Design, Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Leadership and Influence, and Recognition and Reward. Across each segment, meaningful impact is demonstrated through collaboration, partnership and sustained engagement with academics, students and institutional stakeholders. Together, the segments provide a structured approach to evidencing the breadth, depth and relational impact of LD practice. This interactive poster invites the ASCILITE community to inform what constitutes meaningful evidence of LD impact, drawing on diverse institutional contexts and practices across the sector. The poster itself is designed to be conversational, inviting delegates to contribute their perspectives by responding to three reflective prompts: What evidence do you think demonstrates the value of relationships and human connection in LD? What contributions of LDs have you noticed are often overlooked or invisible? What evidence do you see as most important in the future? Using pens and markers, or sticky notes, delegates will collectively build a visual representation of the evidence they value, the invisible work they recognise and the future directions they envision for the profession. This participatory approach reflects the framework’s emphasis on co-creation, reflective practice and shared understanding while creating opportunities for meaningful discussion among delegates from diverse institutional contexts. By the conclusion of the conference, the poster will have evolved into a collective representation of how the LD community values evidence, relationships, and impact. In doing so, it will demonstrate that the future of LD is not defined solely by digital technologies, but by the human connections that enable educational transformation.

Abstract Some environmental regulators now trigger restrictions on forecasts before exceedances occur, while machine-learning methods are proposed for the forecasting pipelines behind them. Delhi-NCR’s Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) directs advance invocation on numerical air-quality forecasts, yet reported practice often followed observed readings. Judicial and regulatory directions demand anticipatory action, yet none reviewed here specifies the confidence a forecast must carry before it justifies coercion. This article asks what validation, reproducibility and uncertainty-quantification thresholds an AI-enabled forecast must meet before triggering binding restrictions. Using a functional comparative method, it separates physics-based forecasts and digital dissemination from the machine-learning layer that makes a pipeline AI-enabled. GRAP, with the Supreme Court’s timing orders, is the single test case. Instruments from India, China, France and California’s air districts are coded for observed, forecast-based and discretionary triggers and read alongside forecast-verification studies. This article argues that proportionality and reasoned decision-making require restrictions to reflect forecast confidence as well as predicted severity, and that precaution licenses early action only if uncertainty is disclosed. One implication is that legal reliance on an AI-enabled forecast should depend on a disclosed validation dossier, because machine-learning layers add opacity and drift. Disclosure supports human oversight and lets affected people contest restrictions built on overconfident models. The contribution is a test mapping calibrated confidence onto the intensity of proportionality review. The assessment is prospective and doctrinal, evaluating design adequacy rather than operational performance; conclusions remain contingent.

The nature of posttraumatic growth (PTG), defined as positive changes that can occur after a traumatic event (TE), is debated due to its complex and dynamic relationship with psychological adjustment. Although heterogeneous PTG trajectories have been identified, the processes underlying their development over time remain insufficiently understood. This study, adopting a person-centred approach, seeks to identify latent classes with distinct multivariate trajectories (PTG, PTSD, positive thinking, deliberate rumination) over 1 year and their sociodemographic, event-related, and psychosocial determinants. A sample of 244 adults exposed to a TE completed, at three points spaced 6 months apart, online questionnaires assessing PTG and psychosocial variables. Sociodemographic and event-related characteristics were collected at baseline. Latent classes with distinct multivariate trajectories were identified. Analyses of variance, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression tested differences between classes and their predictors. Three classes emerged: Constructive PTG (25%), Struggling PTG (45.5%), and No PTG (29.5%). Differences between classes were observed in age, coping, challenge to core beliefs, positive illusions, depression, and social support. Lower baseline adaptive coping predicted membership in the Struggling and No PTG groups, whereas lower challenge to core beliefs predicted the No PTG class. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of trajectories following lifetime trauma and the role of coping and cognitive engagement processes in the evolution of PTG over time. By integrating multiple processes within a longitudinal, person-centred framework, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the perceived PTG.
